idiom_name: state owner fills a `struct view_model`; render-only functions take a `const` pointer to it, events arrive as callback pointers
implementation_notes: C has no component runtime, no props and no re-render step, so the split is a convention between two translation units: one owns the data and its source (socket, file, database handle, device) and fills a snapshot struct, the other contains only functions that format or draw from a `const` pointer to that snapshot and never touch the source. What replaces props is the snapshot itself - passed by const pointer, or by value when small - plus a callback (function pointer with an opaque user-data pointer) for each event the view can raise. The hand-written form is genuinely justified here: when the same renderers must serve a test harness that supplies a literal struct, or when an immediate-mode toolkit already redraws from a snapshot each iteration; where a full toolkit provides its own model/view split, use that instead of hand-writing one.
pitfalls: A renderer that writes to the snapshot or to a global becomes a second owner; take `const` pointers and let the compiler enforce the direction of the dependency.
Nothing re-renders by itself: if the supply half forgets to call the render function after a mutation, the screen keeps showing a stale snapshot.
The user-data pointer of a callback is an untyped lifetime contract - a callback that fires after the canvas or context was freed is a use-after-free.
Format strings assembled from data are an injection hole when the render half emits HTML; route every value through one escape helper.
